Background
Injuries to the thoracolumbar spine usually are the result of substantial blunt trauma,
particularly from high-energy motor vehicle accidents and falls from higher than 6 feet.
Approximately 50% of fractures occur between T11 and L1, and 30% of injuries occur
between L2 and L5.
The high incidence of fractures of the thoracolumbar junction is because of its location at the
biomechanical transition zone between the rigid thoracic rib cage and the more flexible
lumbar spine.1
The spinal canal in the thoracic spine is relatively narrow, increasing the risk of possible
injury-associated compression/neurologic deficits. After a thoracolumbar spine fracture has
been detected, the remaining spine should be imaged to rule out noncontiguous spinal
injury, which may occur in as many as 10.5% of patients; 25% of patients who have spinal
fractures with neurologic deficit have another vertebral injury.2,3
Overview
Fractures of the thoracolumbar spine may be devastating injuries after low- or high-energy
blunt trauma.
Thoracolumbar fractures and dislocations may lead to pain, disability, neurologic deficits, and
posttraumatic deformity (Figures 1 and 2).

Overview
Thoracolumbar spine trauma may affect adult (Resource 1) and pediatric (Resource 2)
patients. The thoracolumbar junction (T10 through L2) is a unique transition zone
between the relatively rigid thoracic spine (T1 through T10) and the more mobile lower

lumbar spine (L3 through L5). At this junction, the spine is subject to great biomechanical
stress and, therefore, the thoracolumbar spine is a common site of failure after blunt
trauma.
Epidemiology
The rate of thoracolumbar fractures after blunt trauma is between 6% and 7%.
Most thoracolumbar fractures occur at the thoracolumbar junction.
Thoracolumbar trauma is associated with spinal cord injury (SCI) and noncontiguous cervical
spine fracture.

Epidemiology
In a meta-analysis, the rate of thoracolumbar fracture in patients who sustained blunt
trauma was 6.9%. The rates of SCI and noncontiguous cervical spine fracture were
26.56% and 10.49%, respectively.4 Therefore, a patient thorough history and physical
examination are essential to rule out injuries to the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine.
In a prospective, cross-sectional study of blunt trauma patients presenting to the
emergency department, thoracolumbar injuries were identified in 6.3% of the patients.
The most common vertebrae involved in descending order were L1, L2, L3, and T12.5 As
many as 50% to 60% of thoracolumbar injuries occurred between T11 and L2, compared
with 25% to 40% in the upper thoracic spine and 10% to 14% in the lower lumbar spine
and sacrum.6 Compression fractures and transverse process fractures were the most
common fracture patterns observed in the thoracic and lumbar spine, respectively.5
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The thoracolumbar spine is divided into the thoracic spine (T1 through T10), thoracolumbar
junction (T10 through L2), and lumbar spine (L3 through L5).
The posterior ligamentous complex (PLC) consists of the facet joint capsule, ligamentum
flavum, interspinous ligament, and supraspinous ligament.
The conus terminalis typically terminates at the L1 vertebral level.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The thoracic spine is a complex three-dimensional structure made up of bones, soft
tissues (intervertebral disks and ligaments), and neural elements (spinal cord and nerve
roots). The thoracolumbar spine can be further divided into the following anatomic
regions: thoracic spine (T1 through T10), thoracolumbar junction (T10 through L2), and
lumbar spine (L3 through L5).
The anatomy of the thoracolumbar spine is best demonstrated by the Denis three-
column principle (Figure 3). According to Denis,7,8 the three columns consist of the
anterior (from the anterior longitudinal ligament to the anterior half of the vertebral
body and disk), middle (from the posterior half of the vertebral body and disk to the
posterior longitudinal ligament), and posterior column (posterior bony elements and
ligamentous complex). The PLC is the capsuloligamentous structures that are essential
for maintaining spinal stability and consist of the facet joint capsule, ligamentum flavum,
interspinous ligament, and supraspinous ligament.
The conus terminalis typically terminates at the L1 vertebral level. Injuries above the
conus may cause thoracic SCI. Injuries at or below the conus may cause conus
medullaris syndrome or cauda equina syndrome, respectively.

The thoracolumbar spine is subjected to different forces with various modes of failure.
Thoracolumbar trauma is most commonly during a motor vehicle collision or a high-energy
fall.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The thoracolumbar spine can fail under supraphysiologic forces in flexion, compression,
extension, distraction, lateral bending, axial rotation, translation, shear, or via a
combination. Katsuura et al4 found motor vehicle collisions (36.7%) and high-energy falls
(31.7%) were the most common etiologies for thoracolumbar trauma. Other less
common etiologies included motorcycle collision, pedestrian struck by a vehicle, or other
etiology (sports-related, industrial, bicyclist injuries).4
Risk Factors
Thoracolumbar trauma in young patients typically is caused by high-energy trauma.
Conversely, thoracolumbar trauma in elderly patients usually is sustained during low-energy
trauma.
Osteopenia and osteoporosis are major risk factors for vertebral compression fractures in
elderly patients.

Risk Factors
Thoracolumbar trauma typically occurs in a bimodal distribution, with higher incidences
reported in males younger than 30 years who sustain high-energy trauma and geriatric
female patients with poor bone mineral density who sustain a low-energy, ground-level
fall.6,9
Cooper et al10 reported that major non-thoracolumbar injuries and a fall mechanism of
injury were considerable risk factors for thoracolumbar trauma after blunt trauma. In
addition, the authors noted that major injuries can impede back pain/tenderness

Therefore, treating providers must be vigilant in the evaluation (Resource 3) of
polytrauma patients with distracting injuries to prevent delayed or missed
thoracolumbar fractures.
As previously mentioned, in elderly patients, osteoporosis is a major risk factor for
thoracolumbar trauma after low-energy mechanisms of injury, such as a fall from
standing height. Osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures affect more than 700,000
Americans annually.12 Therefore, an effective strategy in preventing low-energy
thoracolumbar trauma, such as osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures, is
appropriate diagnosis and management of osteopenia and osteoporosis.
Associated Injuries
Thoracic and lumbar fractures are associated with head, chest, and long bone injuries.
Chance fractures, in particular, are associated with a high risk for intraabdominal injuries.

Associated Injuries
Thoracolumbar trauma may be caused by low- or high-energy blunt trauma. The rate of
associated injuries, especially in patients with a high-energy mechanism of injury, is
substantial.13 Saboe et al13 reported that 82% of thoracic fractures and 72% of lumbar
fractures were associated with other injuries. Most of these injuries involved the head,
chest, or long bones. Katsuura et al4 found the following rates of associated injuries:
abdominal trauma, 7.63%; thoracic trauma, 22.64%; pelvic trauma, 9.39%; extremity
trauma, 18.26%; and head trauma, 12.96%. Flexion-distraction injuries of the
thoracolumbar spine are associated with a high risk for intraabdominal visceral injuries,
with rates as high as 40%.4,14

The two most commonly used thoracolumbar classification systems the Thoracolumbar Injury
Classification and Severity Score (TLICS) and the AOSpine TLICS.
The TLICS is based on injury morphology, integrity of the PLC, and neurologic status (Figure 4).
AOSpine TLICS is based on injury morphology, neurologic status, and two patient-specific
modifiers.
Nonsurgical management is recommended for patients with a TLICS or Thoracolumbar
AOSpine Injury Score (TL AOSIS) of less than or equal to 3.
Surgical management is recommended for patients with a TLICS or TL AOSIS higher than or
equal to 5.
Many classification systems have been proposed for thoracolumbar injuries (Resource 4). The
AOSpine classification system has largely replaced the TLICS and the Denis classification
system (Resource 5).
TLICS was introduced by the Spine Trauma Study Group in 2005 and is based on three
characteristics: injury morphology, integrity of the PLC, and neurologic status15,16 (Resource
6). The injury morphology and integrity of the PLC can be determined based on plain
radiography, CT, and/or MRI. TLICS was the first thoracolumbar injury classification system to
incorporate neurologic status, which is graded based on the American Spinal Injury
Association (ASIA) system. The subgroups in each major variable are assigned points
depending on the extent of involvement or severity. The points from the three variables are
then summed to obtain a comprehensive injury severity score (Resource 7). Nonsurgical
treatment generally is recommended for patients with a combined score of less than or
equal to 3, whereas surgical treatment generally is recommended for patients with a
combined score of higher than or equal to 5.3
The AOSpine TLICS was established in 2013 and relies on injury morphology (A through C),
neurologic status (N), and two patient-specific modifiers (M) to categorize each injury17
(Resource 8).
Classification of the injury morphology is based on three main injury patterns: type A
(compression), type B (tension band disruption), and type C (displacement/translation).
Type A and type B fractures are subclassified more granularly.
A0 = Mechanically unimportant fractures of the spinous or transverse processes
A1 = Fracture of a single end plate without any involvement of the posterior vertebral
wall
A2 = Coronal split or pincer-type fractures involving both end plates, without any
involvement of the posterior vertebral wall

Neurologic status is graded as follows:
N0: no neurologic deficit
N1: transient deficit
N2: radicular symptoms
N3: incomplete SCI or any degree of cauda equina injury
N4: complete SCI
Nx: unknown neurologic status secondary to altered mental status
The two patient-specific modifiers are as follows:
M1 modifier: injury to the posterior tension band is indeterminate
M2 modifier: patient has a comorbidity that argues for or against surgical management
In 2016, Kepler et al18 developed a spine injury score for the AOSpine TLICS called the
Thoracolumbar AOSpine Injury Score (TL AOSIS) (Resource 9). Different points are allocated
for the three major variables of the AOSpine TLICS (ie, injury morphology, neurologic status,
and patient-specific modifiers). Their summation represents the TL AOSIS for a specific
thoracolumbar injury. Nonsurgical treatment is generally recommended for patients with a
TL AOSIS of less than or equal to 3, whereas surgical treatment generally is recommended
for patients with a TL AOSIS higher than or equal to 5.3

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
The initial evaluation of thoracolumbar trauma begins with a thorough patient history and
physical examination.
The initial physical examination should follow Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) guidelines
with assessment of the airway, breathing, and circulation.

Patient History and Physical Examination
A thorough patient history and physical examination in the emergency room is
imperative for timely diagnosis and management of thoracolumbar injuries (Resource
10). The patient history should focus on understanding the mechanism of injury, energy
of the trauma, and symptom severity of the thoracolumbar injuries and associated
injuries. In obtunded patients, the patient history can be obtained from a witness or first
responder.
The initial physical examination follows ATLS principles with assessment of the airway,
breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure (ABCDE). In patients who are able to
participate in the physical examination, a complete assessment of motor and sensory
function should be performed according to the ASIA classification system.19 This
includes assessment of sphincter tone and perianal sensation to determine the presence
or absence of sacral sparing in SCI. The bulbocavernosus reflex should be assessed in
patients in whom SCI is suspected to determine if the patient is in spinal shock.1 Absence
of the bulbocavernosus reflex indicates spinal shock, making the neurologic examination
unreliable. In such situations, the physician must assume an incomplete injury exists
even if the presenting ASIA examination indicates a complete injury. Injuries at the conus
may disrupt the bulbocavernosus reflex, making it unreliable.20
Patients with an upper thoracic SCI also may have disruption of the sympathetic nervous
system, resulting in neurogenic shock and hemodynamic instability.21

Hsu et al22 reported strong associations between thoracolumbar fractures and the
following clinical signs: back pain/midline tenderness, palpable midline step, back
bruising, and abnormal neurologic signs.
Imaging Studies
CT is the initial imaging modality for evaluation of thoracolumbar trauma.
CT of the chest/abdomen/pelvis allows for adequate thoracolumbar evaluation and may
substitute dedicated thoracolumbar CT imaging.
MRI is best for assessing diskoligamentous injuries in the thoracolumbar spine.

Imaging Studies
Although validated decision tools are available to guide the imaging workup for cervical
spine clearance, no such guidelines exist for thoracolumbar imaging after blunt
trauma.23 Although cervical spine imaging is the standard of care after blunt trauma,
imaging of the thoracolumbar spine typically is obtained only if thoracolumbar injury is
suspected based on the patient history and physical examination (Resource 11). In the
work up of polytrauma patients, CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis routinely is
performed; therefore evaluation of the thoracolumbar spine on such CT scans may
afford screening for thoracolumbar spine injuries in patients with blunt trauma.24
Radiography
Plain radiography is less sensitive and specific in detecting thoracolumbar trauma than CT or
MRI.
Upright radiographs can be obtained in the clinic to follow-up after thoracolumbar trauma.

The integrity of the PLC can be inferred from plain radiographs and CT scans, which may
show widening of the interspinous space, facet diastasis, or facet
subluxation/dislocation. Plain radiography is less reliable than CT in detecting and
diagnosing thoracolumbar fractures. A 2018 meta-analysis that reviewed the diagnostic
accuracy of plain radiographs in the detection of thoracolumbar trauma revealed that
the overall pooled sensitivity of five studies for radiography was 61%, with a specificity of
98%. For most of the studies included in the meta-analysis, thoracolumbar CT was
considered the preferred imaging modality.23 Upright plain radiographs can be obtained
to monitor alignment after thoracolumbar trauma. Evidence of instability or progression
of deformity on upright radiographs may indicate surgical management.
CT
CT is considered the preferred imaging modality for the evaluation of thoracolumbar trauma.
The thoracolumbar spine can be thoroughly evaluated with CT scans of the
chest/abdomen/pelvis.

CT
CT, including chest/abdomen/pelvis CT scans and dedicated thoracolumbar CT
reformats, is associated with a much higher sensitivity and specificity than plain
radiography in the detection of thoracolumbar fractures. A pooled analysis of CT scans
among thoracolumbar trauma patients demonstrated a 97% overall sensitivity and 99%
specificity for the detection of thoracolumbar fractures.23 In addition, CT can be
performed more quickly and is less technique dependent than plain radiography or MRI.
Although CT exposes patients to greater radiation levels, potentially increasing the risk
for cancer, CT scans of the CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis often are obtained
when patients are pan-scanned for the workup of traumatic injuries.25 Sagittal CT
reformats are most helpful for assessing overall spinal alignment and fracture patterns;
however, axial and coronal plane reformats also should be performed.

MRI
MRI is most specific and sensitive imaging modality for the detection of soft-tissue injuries,
such as diskoligamentous injury or epidural hematoma.
In general, MRI is recommended in patients with an associated neurologic deficit after
thoracolumbar trauma.
MRI may be useful if suspicion of thoracolumbar injury exists despite normal CT scans or plain
radiographs.

MRI
MRI is associated with a high sensitivity and specificity for the detection of ligamentous
injury, with studies reporting an overall sensitivity of 91% and a specificity of 100% for
the detection of PLC injury in patients with a thoracolumbar fracture.26 MRI provides
important details in the assessment of patients with posttraumatic neurologic deficits,
including patients with injuries at the cord or root level. In addition, MRI may help
determine injury stability and treatment in patients with bony injury and possible
associated ligamentous injuries; this is demonstrated by the inclusion of MRI assessment
of PLC integrity in the TLICS.15-18 However, routine use of MRI for the evaluation of
thoracolumbar trauma is controversial.25 Studies of patients with cervical spine trauma
have shown that MRI may be associated with a high false-positive rate for ligamentous
injury compared with intraoperative findings, and patients with cervical MRI suggestive
of ligamentous injury who have negative CT scans rarely require surgical treatment.25
Appropriate indications for MRI in patients with thoracolumbar trauma include
potentially unstable injury patterns observed on CT scans, patients with neurologic
deficits, and/or obtunded patients I whom concern for neurologic deficits exists.27 In
addition, MRI plays an important role in the work up of patients with ankylosed spines,
such as those with ankylosing spondylitis or diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis
(DISH), because these patients are predisposed to occult fractures and epidural
hematomas with possible neurologic injury.28 In general, practitioners should over-
image patients with substantial ankylosis and altered biomechanics of the spine to
detect occult fractures that may lead to catastrophic neurologic deficit.29

Management
The management of most thoracolumbar fractures is nonsurgical.
The ultimate goals in the management of thoracolumbar fractures is to protect and maintain
neurologic function, prevent the development or progression of spinal deformity, and
maximize patient outcomes. Additional treatment goals include early mobilization to prevent
complications associated with prolonged recumbency, such as pneumonia, urinary tract
infections, pressure wounds, and venous thromboembolism (VTE). Patients who are
neurologically intact, have less than 25° to 35° kyphosis with less than 50% loss of vertebral
height, and less than 50% canal compromise with an intact PLC are the best candidates for
nonsurgical treatment. Standard nonsurgical management often includes hyperextension
thoracolumbar orthoses or cast immobilization for approximately 3 months.
Surgical treatment is indicated for patients with an unstable fracture and/or patients with a
neurologic deficit.
For patients with an incomplete neurologic deficit and ongoing spinal cord compression from
retropulsed fragments, decompression and stabilization typically are required. The selection
of posterior versus anterior decompression and stabilization depends on injury
characteristics. Early stabilization of patients with neurologic injuries facilitates improved
neurologic outcomes, early mobilization, and early rehabilitation.
Patients with unstable burst fractures that include failure of the PLC, fracture-dislocations,
and/or fractures with considerable rotational displacement should undergo initial posterior
stabilization. If correlative neurologic deficits exist in combination with imaging findings of
neural compression, then a posterior-based decompression (laminectomy, transpedicular or
vertebral column resection) with stabilization during the index procedure versus a staged
anterior procedure is warrented.21
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management is recommended for stable thoracolumbar fractures in which the
patient is neurologically intact.
Nonsurgical management is recommended for patients with a TLICS or TL AOSIS of less than
or equal to 3.
Thoracolumbar compression fractures can be nonsurgically managed via symptomatic
management and early mobilization (Figure 5).

Indications
Stable thoracolumbar trauma in patients with normal neurology is managed nonsurgically.
Nonsurgical management is recommended for patients with a TLICS or TL AOSIS of less than
or equal to 3.
Classic compression fractures and burst fractures with normal neurology are managed
nonsurgically.
The retropulsed fragment in a burst fracture can be remodeled or resorbed with time.

Fracture patterns, injury characteristics, associated neurologic injury, and patient
characteristics are important considerations in deciding on nonsurgical versus surgical
management. The TLICS or TL AOSIS may aid in determining which fractures are
amenable to nonsurgical management. Nonsurgical treatment may be appropriate for
patients with a TLICS or TL AOSIS of less than or equal to 3. A TLICS or TL AOSIS of 4 is
indeterminate, and nonsurgical versus surgical management is based on surgeon
discretion. Patients with a TLICS or TL AOSIS higher than or equal to 5 often require
surgical treatment.15,17,18 Patients with considerable canal compromise but who are
neurologically intact may be treated nonsurgically because remodeling and
reconstitution of the spinal canal will occur.30,31
As part of the TLICS or TL AOSIS, fracture morphology and associated spinal stability are
important determinants of nonsurgical versus surgical management. For example, most
compression fractures and stable burst fractures can be managed nonsurgically.
Compression fractures, representing the most common thoracolumbar spine injuries,1
typically are the result of low-energy mechanisms of injury, including flexion and axial
loads in elderly patients and patients with osteoporosis (Figure 6). However,
compression fractures also can occur in young, healthy individuals after higher energy
trauma. Patients who have sustained high-energy trauma are at risk for noncontiguous
spinal injuries; therefore, surgeons must carefully evaluate the entire spine to rule out
additional injuries. Compression fractures only involve the anterior column. Therefore,
most of these patients are stable and can be treated nonsurgically with or without a
brace.

Burst fractures are the second most common thoracolumbar injury pattern (Figure 7).
They represent a severe variant along the spectrum of compression fractures, resulting
from higher energy mechanisms of injury, such as a fall from height or a motor vehicle
collision. Pathognomonic features of burst fractures, as defined by Denis,7 include
vertebral body comminution, increased distance between the pedicles, retropulsion of
the posterior cortex of the vertebral body into the spinal canal, and associated loss of
height of the posterior vertebral body. Therefore, burst fractures represent injury to the
anterior and middle columns. Patients may have considerable spinal canal compromise,
which is best observed on axial CT scans. Canal compromise has been variably shown to
correlate with the presence and severity of neurologic deficits,32,33 with some studies
suggesting that the initial injury, rather than ongoing canal compromise, is responsible
for neurologic deficits.34 Among patients without neurologic deficits, maintained
integrity of the posterior elements confers adequate stability to allow for nonsurgical
management. Even patients with considerable canal compromise may be treated
nonsurgically because remodeling and reconstitution of the spinal canal will occur.30,31

Burst fractures are considered stable if the PLC remains intact. Clues that the PLC is
disrupted include considerable compression exceeding 50% of vertebral body height,
more than 35° of angulation, and neurologic injury.1,35 Although selecting between
surgical and nonsurgical treatment in patients with a burst fracture remains
controversial, clinical and functional outcomes data, including a long-term study by
Wood et al,36 indicate that patients may have superior outcomes if treated nonsurgically.
Wood et al36 randomized patients to surgical or nonsurgical treatment with a brace or
cast, with 16- to 22-year follow-up. Patients treated nonsurgically had better pain,
disability, and functional scores without a substantial difference in kyphosis compared
with those treated surgically. Radiographically, nonsurgically managed burst fractures
often will settle to the initial degree of kyphosis observed immediately postinjury;
however, no relationship between the final degree of kyphosis and clinical outcome has
been observed.1
Flexion-distraction injuries represent an increasing level of injury severity yet may be
amenable to nonsurgical management. Fracture characteristics, patient characteristics,
and concomitant injuries determine whether flexion-distraction injuries can be managed
nonsurgically. Younger patients with a flexion-distraction injury through the bony
elements may be amenable to treatment via hyperextension casting or bracing if no
considerable distraction through the bony elements is present. Conversely, older
individuals and patients with considerable soft-tissue injury involving the
diskoligamentous complex rather than predominantly osseous injuries often require
surgical stabilization to restore the posterior tension band function of the PLC because
ligamentous structures exhibit less potential for healing than bony structures. In
addition, patients with concomitant abdominal, chest, or extremity injuries may require
surgical treatment to allow for appropriate management of other injuries. Patients with
obesity and patients with a rigid kyphotic deformity may require surgical treatment
because their body habitus may prohibit orthotic treatment. One last consideration for
surgical management is injuries around the spinal cord versus the cauda equina given
the potential for catastrophic neurological injury with movement through the fracture.1

equivalent outcomes at 3 months in patients treated with and without a brace with

be obtained with the patient in the designated treatment option (brace or no brace) to

close radiographic follow-up for the first few weeks.

level. Hyperextension braces, such as a Jewett brace, effectively immobilize flexion and

Outcomes
A wide spectrum of injury morphology, patient characteristics, indications, and
treatment modalities complicates the evaluation of treatment outcomes and hinders
direct comparisons between treatment options. Recent improvements in surgical
techniques and instrumentation also complicate the application of historical outcomes
to current clinical practice. An additional barrier to assessing outcomes is the
controversy surrounding spinal injuries that are truly unstable. Therefore, studies have
presented data favoring surgical or nonsurgical management of presumably stable
thoracolumbar injuries. The variability in the literature is reflected by a Cochrane review,
which was unable to find sufficient evidence to support surgical or nonsurgical
management of thoracolumbar burst fractures; however, outcomes data suggest that
patients with a thoracolumbar burst fracture managed nonsurgically may have a lower
risk of complications and lower initial healthcare costs.38 In addition, long-term outcome
data from studies such as Wood et al36 suggest that nonsurgical management may
result in good outcomes over long-term follow-up periods. For example, at final 16- to
22-year follow-up in the cohort examined by Wood et al,36 47% of surgically treated
patients were still fully employed compared with 72% of nonsurgically treated patients.
Similarly, long-term opioid use was lower in the nonsurgical group, with zero patients in
the nonsurgical group and three patients in the surgical group being treated with long-
term opioids.

compression fracture recalcitrant to nonsurgical management.
The surgical approach (anterior, posterior, or combined) typically depends on fracture
morphology.

Indications
Surgical treatment is indicated in patients with thoracolumbar trauma and neurologic
deficits and patients with an unstable fracture pattern as demonstrated by severe
kyphosis of greater than >35°, PLC injury, and severe canal compromise (usually
considered to be >50%). In addition, surgical treatment is indicated in patients who are
unable to tolerate orthosis wear or cast immobilization because of polytrauma, obesity,
wounds, or skin lesions, and to facilitate early mobilization in patients with other
extremity injuries.35,39 Special consideration and attention to detail must be given to
patients with a stiff spine (ankylosing spondylitis or DISH) and subtle three-column
fractures with a low threshold for surgical treatment. The principal advantages of
surgical management include ability to restore spinal stability, sagittal balance, and
patency of the spinal canal.
Specific indications for surgical treatment vary based on fracture morphology,
particularly in patients without neurologic deficits. For example, although most
compression fractures are managed nonsurgically, AO type A2 compression fractures
with a split component may require surgical stabilization to prevent painful nonunion.1

Patients with an ankylosed spine as a result of DISH or ankylosing spondylitis represent

Preoperative Planning
Many factors affect which patients are treated surgical, the timing of surgical treatment,
and which procedures are perform. Careful assessment of preoperative imaging studies,
neurologic examination findings, injury morphology and characteristics, and patient
characteristics is crucial for effective preoperative planning. The goals of any surgical
procedure should be clearly defined; these may include neurologic decompression,
spinal stabilization, deformity prevention, or pain control for early mobilization. The
presence of neurologic deficits increases the urgency of surgical management,9,49

level of comfort with implant systems. Surgeons also must consider if neuromonitoring
is necessary based on injury level, injury characteristics, and the presence of neurologic
injury, among other factors. Preoperative planning also should account for postoperative
management, including postoperative mobilization and rehabilitation.

injury, whereas AO type C injuries typically necessitate fusion two levels above and two
levels below the level of injury. Additional augmentation may be performed via hooks
and sublaminar fixation with bands and wires to reduce stress on pedicle screws and
reduce the risk of adjacent segment disease. Conversely, greater rigidity of the thoracic
spine permits longer fusion constructs, typically spanning three levels above and three
levels below the level of injury. Arthrodesis in the thoracolumbar spine is augmented
with the use of local bone graft from resected spinous processes and also may be
augmented with the use of other autogenous bone graft, such as iliac crest or
autologous bone graft.21
Postoperative Management
The goal of postoperative management is early mobilization to prevent complications
associated with prolonged recumbency.
Mechanical and chemical VTE prophylaxis generally is recommended if no contraindication is
present.
Antibiotic agents are routinely administered within 1 hour before incision and are continued
24 hours postoperatively.

Postoperative Management
Overall, evidence for many aspects of postoperative management among the
thoracolumbar spine trauma population is lacking. This may be because considerable
heterogeneity exists among the thoracolumbar spine trauma population. Therefore,
postoperative treatment for patients with a thoracolumbar spine fracture depends on
the injury type, the surgical procedures performed, the presence of neurologic deficits
and concomitant injuries, surgeon experience, and local practice patterns. Collaboration
with other specialties, including general surgery, orthopedic trauma, and physiatrists, is
necessary to optimize patient rehabilitation.

Patients with a spinal injury are at high risk for VTE,55,56 and guidelines recommend that
patients receive postoperative VTE prophylaxis via mechanical VTE prophylaxis,
unfractionated heparin, or low-molecular-weight heparin.57,58 Early initiation of VTE
prophylaxis (within 48 hours postoperatively) may safely reduce the rate of deep vein
thrombosis in patients with a spinal fracture.59
Patient with spinal trauma have a higher risk for infection than patients who undergo
elective spine surgery.60 The North American Spine Society recommends perioperative
antibiotic agents for patients undergoing instrumented fusion and suggests that patients
undergoing surgical treatment for the management of spinal trauma may benefit from
prolonged postoperative antibiotic regimens.61 However, high-quality evidence to guide
postoperative antibiotic prophylaxis and the duration of postoperative antibiotic
prophylaxis in thoracolumbar trauma patients is lacking.62
Postoperative treatment for patients with a spinal fracture also should focus on early
mobilization to decrease the risks associated with prolonged recumbency, including
pneumonia, urinary tract infection, and pressure wounds. Multimodal pain control may
be beneficial in reducing the risks associated with narcotics. Finally, postoperative full-
length plain radiographs allow for assessment of vertebral alignment and proper
placement of instrumentation and provide baseline imaging studies for comparison at
clinic follow-up.
Complications
Thoracolumbar fractures are associated with severe medical and surgical complications.
Early mobilization is encouraged to prevent complications associated with prolonged
recumbency, such as pulmonary infection or VTE.
Complication rates among patients with thoracolumbar trauma who are treated surgically or
nonsurgically are difficult to determine given the heterogeneity of injury patterns,
concomitant injuries, and difficulty with long-term follow-up63 (Resource 18). Patients
treated surgically are subject to typical complications associated with thoracolumbar
decompression and fusion, including infection, neurologic injury, instrumentation failure,
pseudarthrosis, and adjacent segment disease (Resource 19). Patients with spinal trauma

In addition, with limited outcomes data available to guide treatment, patients with spinal

managed nonsurgically or fusion across longer segments than necessary. Patients with spine
trauma also are at risk of medical complications, such as pulmonary complications and VTE.
Overall complication rates, including surgical and medical complications, likely are influenced
by the presence of neurologic injury.63
Although limited data are available regarding complication rates in patients with
thoracolumbar trauma, a 2014 literature review of complications in surgically or
nonsurgically managed thoracolumbar AO type A3 burst fractures reported an overall
complication rate of 32.6% among surgically treated patients and 4.8% among nonsurgically
treated patients. The overall infection rate was higher in surgically treated patients. The
surgical group also had a 4.35% incidence of instrumentation failure necessitating revision
surgery. Additional complications observed included pulmonary complications; VTE;
infections, including pulmonary nodular amyloidosis, urinary tract infections, and wound
complications; cardiac complications; and gastrointestinal complications. The authors further
concluded that, although surgical management is often recommended to reduce
complications related to prolonged recumbency, aggregated study results suggest that
surgically treated patients may have a higher risk for complications frequently attributed to
prolonged recumbency.63
Specific patient populations are subject to unique complications. For example, patients with
neurologic injury have additional risks unique to neurologic deficit, including pressure
wounds and complications related to loss of protective sensation and loss of voluntary bowel
and bladder function. Patients treated via cement augmentation for the management of a
compression fracture, including vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty, are at risk of cement
extravasation, with subsequent impingement and compression of neural structures, and
cement embolism into the vasculature, resulting in pulmonary emboli.46
Outcomes
Complications are higher in patients with a thoracolumbar fracture that is managed surgically
compared with nonsurgically because of the inherent risks associated with surgical treatment.
Careful patient selection, thorough preoperative planning, meticulous surgical execution, and
early postoperative mobilization may optimize outcomes and minimize complications.

Management of thoracolumbar trauma fractures remains controversial, particularly because
no large, randomized trials have been conducted to evaluate treatment outcomes. In
addition, much of the existing data are contradictory. Regarding burst fracture management
in neurologically stable patients, Wood et al36 reported that 71% of patients treated
nonsurgically for a thoracolumbar burst fracture were able to return to work within 6
months, whereas 42% of patients treated surgically returned to work within 6 months. Of the
14 surgically treated patients who eventually returned to work, 8 returned to a similar job. In
comparison, 15 of 17 nonsurgically treated patients who eventually returned to work
returned to a similar job. Complications were substantially different between surgically and
nonsurgically treated patients; 19 complications occurred among 16 patients treated
surgically, whereas 2 complications occurred among the 24 patients treated nonsurgically. At
final long-term follow-up over 16 to 22 years in the cohort studied by Wood et al,36 47% of
patients treated surgically were still fully employed, and 72% of patients treated
nonsurgically were still fully employed. In addition, three surgically treated patients and zero
nonsurgically treated patients were being treated with opioids at final follow-up.36 The
results from the study by Wood et al36 study are similar to those of the case series
performed by McLain,64 which included 68 surgically treated patients, among whom a 19%
revision surgery rate was reported. Overall, 58% of patients in the series were pain-free at
final follow-up, 56% had no functional limitations compared with their preoperative status,
77% were working full-time or considered able to work full-time, and 53% returned to their
previous level of employment. This study cohort primarily included young, healthy males,
and neurologic recovery was the primary determinant of functional outcomes, including
return to work.64
Pearls and Pitfalls
CT, often performed during the initial assessment of trauma patients, plays an important role
in identifying and characterizing traumatic thoracolumbar injuries.
Most thoracolumbar compression and burst fractures can be managed nonsurgically.
Nonsurgical management often consists of hyperextension thoracolumbar orthosis wear.
Important indications for surgical treatment in patients with thoracolumbar trauma include
neurologic deficits;, unstable fracture patterns; and severe deformity, often defined as
kyphosis greater than 35° and PLC injury, severe canal compromise, and inability to tolerate
orthosis wear.

Careful preoperative planning is crucial for successful surgical management of thoracolumbar
trauma. Surgical management may be performed via a posterior, anterior, or combined
approach, all of which allow for neural decompression and spinal fusion. Surgeons must
carefully select segments for fusion to maintain motion and ensure adequate stability.
Patients with posttraumatic neurologic deficits should have a mean arterial pressure above 85
mm Hg; however, evidence does not support the use of corticosteroid therapy for promoting
neurologic recovery.
Complication and outcome data are limited among the thoracolumbar trauma patient
population, and patients are subject to unique complications based on their injury patterns.
